opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it is that we're not trying to build a single model that solves one narrow problem in drug discovery. The ambition is really to build a general drug design engine, something that can work across many different therapeutic areas, many different target classes, and eventually many different drug modalities, whether that's small molecules or beyond.

If you look at how drug discovery has traditionally worked, it's very bespoke. Every new program, every new target, you're almost starting from scratch, with a lot of wet lab iteration, a lot of trial and error, and a lot of human intuition guiding which molecules to make next. What we want to do is move a huge part of that process into the computer, so that you can reason about biology and chemistry in silico, rapidly design and evaluate candidate molecules, and only go to the lab to validate the most promising ideas.

To do that, you need a whole suite of capabilities working together. Structure prediction is a big piece of it, and that's where the AlphaFold lineage comes in, understanding how proteins look and how molecules interact with them. But that's only the starting point. You also need to predict things like binding affinity, selectivity, how a molecule will behave in the body, its toxicity, whether it can actually be synthesized. And then you need generative capabilities that can propose new molecules that satisfy all of those constraints at once.

So the scope is really end to end. We think of it as building a set of models that together form something like a design engine, where you can pose a question, say "I want a molecule that hits this target, avoids these off-targets, and has these properties," and the system helps you search that enormous chemical space intelligently.

And the reason we believe this is the right scope is generality. The more general the engine, the more it benefits from scale and from learning across problems. Every program we work on teaches the system something that makes it better on the next one. That's quite different from the traditional model, and it's what we think could ultimately change the speed and success rate of discovering new medicines.

r001.rationale: The response describes the ambition as a general drug-design engine that works across many therapeutic areas and learns across programs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that we're not trying to build a tool that helps with one step of drug discovery. We're trying to build an engine that models the whole thing, from the biology of a disease all the way through to a molecule you can actually give to a patient.

If you look at how drugs are made today, it's an enormously fragmented process. You have one group doing target identification, another doing structural biology, another doing medicinal chemistry, another worrying about toxicity and pharmacokinetics. Each of those steps has its own experts, its own tooling, its own intuitions, and information gets lost at every handoff. The chemist optimizing potency doesn't have a great model of what's going to happen in the liver. The biologist picking the target doesn't have a strong sense of whether that target is even druggable.

So the ambition is to have a single system, or really a family of models that talk to each other, that can reason across all of those layers at once. That starts with structure, which is where AlphaFold gave us a foundation. But structure alone isn't a drug. You need to understand how a small molecule or an antibody binds, how strongly, how selectively, what else in the body it might hit, how it behaves once it's absorbed. Each of those is a prediction problem, and each one has historically been attacked in isolation with fairly narrow models.

What's changed is that we now believe you can learn these things jointly, and that learning them jointly makes each one better. The same way large language models got good at a lot of tasks by being trained on everything rather than on one task at a time, we think a drug design engine gets more powerful when physics, chemistry, and biology are all represented in the same system and can inform one another.

The other piece of scope that matters to me is generality. We don't want something that works on kinases and nothing else. We want to be able to point this at a target class nobody has successfully drugged before and have a real shot. That's the test. If the engine only reproduces what medicinal chemists already know how to do, we haven't built anything interesting. The whole point is to go after the ninety percent of biology that's currently considered undruggable.

And then, honestly, the long-term scope is to compress the whole cycle. Right now it takes a decade and billions of dollars to get a drug to patients, and most of them fail. If you can make the design phase dramatically faster and the failure rate dramatically lower, you change what's economically possible. Diseases that are too rare or too hard to justify a program today suddenly become tractable. That's the frame I keep coming back to. It's not a better hammer. It's a different way of doing the whole thing.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a general engine spanning disease biology through drug design, and says it should work across target classes, including previously undrugged biology. This communicates broad reuse across disease areas.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as building a general engine for drug design. You want to be able to give it a biological target and the properties you need from a drug, and then design a molecule that satisfies those requirements.

That’s a much broader problem than predicting whether a molecule binds to a protein. Binding matters, but so do selectivity, toxicity, whether the molecule gets to the right place in the body, and how long it stays there. Those properties interact, so the challenge is to reason about them together rather than optimize each one independently.

The ambition is for that capability to generalize across different targets and disease areas. Experiments would still be essential, both to test the designs and to improve the models. But you’d like to move more of the search into computation, so that when you make and test a molecule, you’re doing it with a much stronger understanding of why it should work.

r001.rationale: The response describes building a general drug-design engine and says its capability should generalize across different targets and disease areas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as trying to build a general engine for drug design. You want to be able to take a biological hypothesis—a particular target you believe could affect a disease—and design a molecule that actually becomes a useful medicine.

That’s a much broader problem than predicting a protein structure or finding a molecule that binds to a protein. Binding is one requirement, but you also need selectivity, the right behavior in the body, and safety. Those properties interact, so the challenge is to reason about them together rather than optimize each one in isolation.

The ambition is to bring those pieces into a unified computational system, with experiments providing feedback. You design molecules, test them, learn from the results, and use that learning to make the next designs better. Ultimately, we want that engine to generalize across different targets and therapeutic areas, so that each new drug discovery program benefits from what the system has learned before.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general drug-design engine intended to generalize across targets and therapeutic areas, with each new program benefiting from prior learning.
